moduleTitle: Karma, rebirth and the aim of mukti

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.1 Key beliefs: beliefs in karma and rebirth, and the aim of mukti; the meaning of mukti, including the different aspects of mukti – positive and negative.
note.summary:
KARMA
Karma means 'action' and the law of cause and effect. Every action has consequences, in this life and beyond. Japji Sahib says 'You shall harvest what you plant' ('Aape beej aape hi khaahu', pauri 20, Ang 4). Good actions bring spiritual progress; selfish actions driven by haumai and the five thieves bring suffering and further births.

REBIRTH (transmigration / samsara)
The soul (atma) is eternal and passes from body to body. The Guru Granth Sahib speaks of the soul wandering through 8.4 million (chaurasi lakh) life forms. Karma decides the body one is born into: 'By the karma of past actions, the robe of this physical body is obtained; by God's grace, the gate of liberation is found' (Japji pauri 4, Ang 2). Human birth is rare and is the opportunity to escape the cycle (Ang 12).

GRACE AND KARMA
Unlike some ideas of karma as a fixed machine, Sikhism teaches that God's grace (nadar, kirpa, Gurprasad) can overcome karma. Meditation on the Name, the Guru's teaching and the sangat help wash away the effects of past karma. Karma explains the body we have; grace opens the door to mukti.

MUKTI – THE AIM OF LIFE
Mukti means liberation. It has two aspects:
• NEGATIVE aspect – what one is freed FROM: the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; the bondage of karma; haumai, maya and the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment, pride).
• POSITIVE aspect – what one gains: union with God, merging with God's light like a drop of water with the ocean; living in God's presence and bliss (anand); reaching Sach Khand (realm of truth, Japji pauri 37, Ang 8).

JIVAN MUKTI
Sikhs believe mukti can be achieved while still alive (jivan mukt). A jivan mukt person lives in the world as a householder, but free from ego, constantly remembering God and serving others. This makes mukti something that shapes everyday life, not just life after death.

HOW TO ACHIEVE MUKTI
Grace of God; nam japna; becoming gurmukh; sewa; kirat karna; vand chhakna; the company of the sangat; progressing through the five khands.

DIVERSITY
Sikhs differ on how literally to take the 8.4 million life forms and heaven/hell imagery – some see them as real states, others as symbolic of a soul's closeness or distance from God. Humanists reject rebirth, arguing this is our only life; some critics argue karma can be misused to justify inequality, which the Gurus opposed.

KEY TERMS: karma, atma, samsara/transmigration, chaurasi lakh, nadar, Gurprasad, mukti, jivan mukti, Sach Khand, anand.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is the Sikh term for liberation from the cycle of rebirth and union with God?
A Mukti
B Maya
C Manmukh
D Moh
questions.modelAnswer: A – Mukti. Mukti means liberation: freedom from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth and union with God. Maya is illusion, manmukh means self-centred, and moh is worldly attachment.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
Which one of the following is described as a 'positive' aspect of mukti?
A Escaping the cycle of rebirth
B Being freed from the effects of karma
C Union with God and living in God's presence
D No longer being reborn as an animal
questions.modelAnswer: C – Union with God and living in God's presence. The 'negative' aspect of mukti is what a person is freed from (rebirth, karma, haumai); the 'positive' aspect is what they gain – merging with God like a drop of water returning to the ocean, and enjoying God's presence and bliss.
evidence: Positive and negative aspects of mukti
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one meaning of the term 'karma' in Sikhism.
questions.modelAnswer: The law of cause and effect: a person's actions (good or bad) have consequences in this life and determine the form of their next birth.
evidence: 'Aape beej aape hi khaahu' – Japji pauri 20, Ang 4
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give one thing that Sikhs believe is needed to achieve mukti.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: God's grace (nadar/Gurprasad); meditation on God's Name (nam japna); overcoming haumai; following the Guru's teaching/becoming gurmukh; doing sewa; living virtuously.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in karma influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Sikhs try to act well, knowing their actions have consequences. Since 'you shall harvest what you plant' (Ang 4), a Sikh will try to be honest, generous and kind, for example by giving dasvandh (a tenth of income) to help others.

Second way: Sikhs accept responsibility for their own lives rather than blaming others. Belief in karma encourages them to reflect on their behaviour and to change, because good actions and God's grace can improve their spiritual state and lead them towards a better rebirth or mukti.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the belief in mukti influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: It gives Sikhs a goal for their lives. Because the aim is union with God, Sikhs prioritise daily prayer and nam japna, such as reciting Nitnem and meditating on 'Waheguru', rather than chasing wealth or fame.

Second way: Belief in jivan mukti (liberation while still alive) encourages Sikhs to live as gurmukh now, not just to hope for a reward after death. They try to serve others and overcome ego in daily life, for example through sewa in the langar, because a liberated person lives selflessly in the world.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about karma and rebirth.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Karma is the law that actions have consequences. Good actions lead to good results and selfish actions to suffering, both in this life and in future lives. A soul's karma decides which life form it is born into next.

Second teaching: Karma can be overcome by God's grace. Sikhs believe that karma does not lock a person in forever: through God's grace (nadar), meditation on the Name and following the Guru, a person's karma can be cleansed and the cycle of rebirth (samsara/transmigration) can end.

Source: Japji Sahib pauri 4 (Ang 2) says 'By the karma of past actions, the robe of this physical body is obtained; by God's grace, the gate of liberation is found'. This applies both teachings: karma decides the body we are born into, but grace opens the way to mukti.
evidence: 'Karmee aavai kaprra nadree mokh duaar' – Japji pauri 4, Ang 2
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two aspects of mukti in Sikh teaching.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First aspect (negative – what one is freed from): Mukti is liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth, and from the bondage of karma, haumai and the five thieves. The soul no longer has to wander through many life forms.

Second aspect (positive – what one gains): Mukti is union with God, like a drop of water merging back into the ocean. The liberated soul experiences God's eternal presence and bliss (anand), and some Sikhs speak of reaching Sach Khand, the realm of truth. This can begin in this life – jivan mukti.

Source: The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that the light of the liberated soul merges into God's light, as water mingles with water. Japji pauri 37 (Ang 8) describes Sach Khand as the realm where 'the Formless Lord abides', showing mukti is a positive state of being with God, not just an escape.
evidence: Japji pauri 37, Ang 8 – 'Sach khand vasai nirankar'

questions.question:
“Mukti depends on God's grace, not on a person's actions.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Sikh scripture strongly emphasises grace. Japji Sahib says 'By the karma of actions the body is obtained; by grace (nadar) the gate of liberation is found' (Ang 2). The Mool Mantra ends with Gurprasad – God is known by the Guru's grace. This suggests that no amount of good deeds can earn mukti; it is God's free gift.

Sikhs believe that relying on one's own actions can increase haumai, the very ego that blocks mukti. If people think they have earned liberation by their good works, they become proud. Recognising dependence on grace keeps a Sikh humble.

Guru Nanak criticised people who thought rituals, pilgrimages or fasting would earn salvation. Only God's grace, not outward actions, transforms the heart.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Sikhs also believe strongly in karma: 'You shall harvest what you plant' (Ang 4). A person's actions shape their life and rebirths, so actions clearly matter. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that one who does sewa in this world receives a place of honour in God's court (Ang 26).

The three pillars – nam japna, kirat karna and vand chhakna – are all actions. A manmukh who ignores God and lives selfishly is not liberated, whereas a gurmukh who meditates and serves is. So many Sikhs argue that grace and actions work together: God's grace is given to those who turn to God, and grace in turn enables good actions.

The five khands also suggest progress through effort: duty (Dharam Khand), knowledge (Gian Khand) and effort (Saram Khand) come before grace (Karam Khand) and truth (Sach Khand). Effort leads to the stage where grace is received. A non-religious person might reject both ideas but argue that what matters morally is people's actions.

CONCLUSION

Sikhism clearly teaches that mukti is ultimately a gift of grace – the 'gate of liberation' is opened by God's nadar. But it equally insists on effort: meditation, honest work, sharing and sewa prepare the person to receive grace. The best judgement is that the statement is half right: mukti depends on grace, but grace is not separate from a God-centred life of action.
questions.examTip: Use the four bullets: refer to Sikh teaching, argue for the statement, argue for a different view, and reach a justified conclusion. Develop each argument into a chain of reasoning (because... this means... therefore...). Up to 3 extra SPaG marks are available, so use specialist Punjabi terms accurately.

questions.question:
“Belief in rebirth makes people care less about this life.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Some critics argue that if people believe they will be reborn, they may not take this life so seriously, thinking they will have another chance. They might also accept suffering or injustice as the result of past karma instead of trying to change things.

Humanists and atheists argue that because this is the only life we have, people should make the most of it and work to improve the world now. On this view belief in rebirth risks distracting people from present responsibilities.

There have been times in history when belief in karma has been used to justify inequality, for example by saying someone was born into a 'low' caste because of past karma – an attitude the Gurus rejected but which still affects some communities.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Sikhs believe the human birth is rare and precious: 'This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe' (Ang 12). Belief in rebirth makes this life more important, not less, because wasting it may mean many more lives in other forms before the soul has another chance.

Belief in karma also encourages responsibility: 'You shall harvest what you plant' (Ang 4). Sikhs therefore try to act justly now. The emphasis on jivan mukti – liberation while alive – means Sikhs aim to become God-centred in this life, not postpone it.

Sikh practice is very this-worldly. Kirat karna (honest work), vand chhakna (sharing) and sewa all focus on the present. Sikhs are householders, not monks, and the Gurus fought injustice in this world – Guru Tegh Bahadur was martyred defending religious freedom. Sikh charities such as Khalsa Aid show active concern for people suffering now.

CONCLUSION

Belief in rebirth could, in theory, make people complacent, but in Sikhism it does the opposite: the human life is the special opportunity for union with God, and karma means every action counts. Sikh teaching and practice focus strongly on the present life. So, at least for Sikhs, the statement is not convincing; belief in rebirth increases the value of this life.
